 Society | Published 2026.11.08. 01:00:05 | By Kim Do-yeon doremi@sedaily.com | Summary | Save A A A A police officer carries an elderly man on his back after rescuing him from a rain-soaked hillside where he had lost his way. Captured from the "Korean National Police Agency" YouTube channel "Ma'am! Can you hear us?" An elderly woman who lost her way on a rain-soaked hillside during a typhoon was rescued safely after a persistent search by police officers.
 The Korean National Police Agency recently posted footage on its official YouTube channel, "Korea National Police Agency," showing officers locating and rescuing an elderly woman who had gotten lost on a hillside in Gwangju on the 25th of last month.
 Police received a report at the time saying the woman was lost in the mountains and did not know where she was. Heavy rain from the typhoon and falling temperatures meant any delay in the rescue could have put her in danger.
 The officers dispatched to the scene searched the mountainside, repeatedly calling out, "Ma'am! Can you hear us?" Pushing through paths tangled with vines and thorn bushes, they tore their clothes and took thorns to the skin. One officer said, "My clothes are getting torn," and "I'm going to tumble down," but pressed on, saying, "Let's search a bit more. We're almost there."
 As the officers pushed vines aside with umbrellas and their hands, a faint voice came from somewhere. They moved toward the sound, called out again and finally found her.
 One officer checked the scratches the thorns had left on her and comforted her, saying, "You must have been pricked by thorns too, ma'am. You've been through a lot." She thanked the officers.
 The rescue did not end there. Coming back down the steep, rain-slicked trail was no easy task either.
 "Hold on to me, ma'am. Grab my back," the officers said as they supported her. With her strength gone, two officers took turns carrying her down the mountain on their backs. They then handed her over to a paramedic team that had been called in advance so she could receive emergency care.
 Senior Inspector Yang Dong-ho of the support substation at Gwangju Dongbu Police Station, who took part in the rescue, said, "I gave it everything I had to the end, with the mindset that I was searching for my own family." He added, "When the public needs help, the Korean police will never give up — we will search to the end and stay with them to the end."
